name: Prehistory & Ancient Near East
introduction: The earliest archaeological and artistic traces of felids in human culture reveal the dawn of feline representation and domestication across the Paleolithic world, the Fertile Crescent, and the Mediterranean basin. From Ice Age mammoth-ivory carvings and cave murals to Neolithic human-cat burials in Cyprus, enthroned felines at Çatalhöyük, and sacred processional reliefs in Babylon and Persia, cats crossed the threshold from revered primeval apex predator to domestic guardian and spiritual companion.

name: Paleolithic & Neolithic Art and Sculpture
introduction: The earliest manifestations of human visual culture, featuring mammoth-ivory carvings, parietal cave murals of cave lions, and Neolithic terracotta figurines.

name: Ancient Egypt
introduction: In ancient Egyptian civilization, the domestic cat (miu) occupied a unique intersection of domestic affection, practical necessity, and cosmic theology. Revered as manifestations of the goddess Bastet and the solar defender Ra against the serpent Apep, felines were depicted in tomb wall paintings, sacred temple bronzes, and loving domestic reliefs.

name: Classical Antiquity
introduction: Throughout the Greco-Roman world and Etruscan Italy, cats were recognized as exotic companions, agile vermin hunters, and symbols of luxury and domestic independence. Preserved across Pompeian floor mosaics, Attic red-figure vases, funerary stelae, and coins of Magna Graecia, classical feline imagery captures tension, agility, and playful observation.

name: Medieval Europe
introduction: The medieval European imagination viewed the cat with intense ambivalence: cherished by monastic scribes for guarding precious manuscripts from rodents, yet occasionally demonized in theological folklore as nocturnally uncanny. Scribes and illuminators celebrated cats in bestiaries and illuminated margins (drolleries), capturing their absurd acrobatics, mouse-hunting heroics, and humorous subversions.

name: Indigenous Americas & Pre-Columbian Civilizations
introduction: Across Mesoamerica, Central America, and the Andean highlands, pre-Columbian cultures (Olmec, Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú, Maya, and Inca) revered wild felines as sacred embodiments of shamanic transformation, celestial power, and underworld guardianship.

name: East Asian Traditions
introduction: In the visual traditions of China, Korea, and Japan, cats were celebrated as emblems of longevity, domestic serenity, and supernatural whimsy. Imperial Chinese scrolls, Korean Joseon masterworks, and Japanese Edo ukiyo-e woodblocks elevated feline observation into high artistic refinement and popular visual culture.

name: The Islamic World
introduction: In Islamic civilization, cats enjoyed affection and ritual purity, celebrated in Hadith traditions honoring the Prophet Muhammad's tenderness toward felines like Muezza. Across Persian, Mughal, and Ottoman court painting, cats appear in moral animal allegories such as Kalila wa Dimna, intimate dervish hermitages, and opulent palace terraces.

name: The Renaissance
introduction: The European Renaissance re-engaged with direct empirical observation and humanistic symbolism, casting cats in complex dual roles. While Leonardo da Vinci dissected the mechanical elegance of feline muscles and movement, painters like Lotto, Veronese, and Dürer wove cats into sacred scenes as symbols of domestic intimacy, sensory distraction, or theological tension.

name: The Baroque & Dutch Golden Age
introduction: The seventeenth century witnessed the triumph of genre painting and naturalistic still life across the Low Countries, Spain, and Italy. Felines became central actors in domestic comedies of misrule, moralizing proverbs, kitchen pantries, and exquisite monumental engravings celebrating the psychological presence of the domestic cat.

name: The Eighteenth Century
introduction: The Enlightenment and Rococo eras transformed the domestic cat into an emblem of bourgeois refinement, feminine intimacy, and biting social satire. From Chardin's visceral still lifes and Perronneau's luminous pastels to Hogarth's cautionary London moralities and Goya's nocturnal tensions, cats reflected the anxieties and luxuries of the age.

name: The Nineteenth Century
introduction: The nineteenth century brought unprecedented aesthetic diversification. Cats evolved from wild predator studies in Romanticism to shocking symbols of modernity in Manet's Olympia, sentimental Victorian salon spectacles by Henriëtte Ronner-Knip, Impressionist domestic companions, and iconic Bohemian poster art of Montmartre.

name: Early Twentieth Century
introduction: The opening decades of the twentieth century dismantled classical illusionism, rendering the cat through daring Fauvist colour, expressive distortion, Ashcan realism, and psychological abstraction. Artists from Franz Marc to Gwen John, Paul Klee, and Tsuguharu Foujita celebrated the cat as an autonomous spirit of feline instinct and modernist design.

name: Mid-Twentieth Century & Modernism
introduction: Spanning Surrealism, mid-century sculpture, and postwar expressive figuration, mid-20th-century masters turned to the feline as an emblem of psychic mystery, existential tension, and totemic companionship.

name: New Kingdom Daily Life & Tomb Murals
introduction: During the New Kingdom, cats were painted beneath chairs in banqueting scenes and depicted accompanying elite hunters into marshlands, embodying both playful companionship and protective solar energy.

name: Late Period & Ptolemaic Votive Bronzes
introduction: The Late and Ptolemaic periods saw the flowering of the cult of Bastet at Bubastis, producing exquisite hollow-cast bronze statuettes, mummies in woven linen coffins, and votive amulets dedicated by pious pilgrims.

name: Greco-Roman Mosaics, Frescoes & Pottery
introduction: In Magna Graecia and Roman Campania, mosaicists and vase painters recorded domestic cats with sharp naturalism, stalking birds in dining-room floor tesserae or serving as luxury pets on funerary monuments.

name: Manuscript Illumination & Bestiaries
introduction: Monastic scriptoriums produced rich moralizing bestiary miniatures and irreverent marginal drolleries where cats hunt mice, play musical instruments, or lick their hind legs beside sacred texts.

name: Gothic Carvings, Misericords & Tapestries
introduction: In cathedral choir stalls and aristocratic tapestries, woodcarvers and weavers inserted cats as folkloric symbols of the 'world upside down', deceit, or quiet domestic fireside warmth.

name: Chinese Han, Song & Qing Painting & Decorative Arts
introduction: Chinese court and literati painters rendered cats (mao) with brushwork of breathtaking delicacy, often pairing them with butterflies (die) to create visual puns wishing octogenarian longevity (maodie).

name: Joseon Dynasty Korean Painting
introduction: Joseon artists, led by the renowned 'Byeon the Cat' (Byeon Sang-byeok) and Kim Hong-do, painted cats in rural gardens, balancing hair-thin anatomical realism with vibrant genre humor.

name: Japanese Edo & Meiji Ukiyo-e
introduction: In the floating world of Edo, masters like Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Hiroshige, and Yoshitoshi turned the cat into a superstar of woodblock prints: anthropomorphized kabuki actors, spirit-monsters, and beloved studio companions.

name: Islamic Miniatures, Ceramics & Metalwork
introduction: From the fables of Kalila wa Dimna to Mughal imperial court albums and Ottoman market chronicles, miniaturists depicted cats as contemplative companions to dervishes and pampered palace pets.

name: Italian Renaissance & Mannerism
introduction: Italian masters analyzed the cat's serpentine anatomy through rigorous draftsmanship, while placing cats at religious feasts and annunciations as dynamic counterweights of everyday life.

name: Northern Renaissance
introduction: In Flanders and Germany, Dürer, Cranach, and Netherlandish masters deployed the cat within complex moral emblems and humoral theories, embodying the phlegmatic temperament and predatory cunning.

name: Dutch Golden Age Genre & Still Life
introduction: Dutch artists celebrated the domestic cat as an unruly household presence: stealing food from distracted maids, enduring children's mock dance lessons, and sitting regally in monumental etchings.

name: Flemish Baroque & Animal Allegory
introduction: In Antwerp, Jan van Kessel, Frans Snyders, and the Teniers workshop staged dramatic pantry fights, cat concerts, and anthropomorphic barber shops highlighting animal instinct and comedic allegory.

name: Italian, Spanish & French Baroque
introduction: Velázquez, Zurbarán, and Carracci brought quiet gravitas to felines: curling peacefully in the foreground of royal workshops or engaging in tense street-corner psychological confrontations.

name: French Rococo & Domestic Genre
introduction: Chardin captured the wild, bristling ferocity of cats in still life, while Fragonard, Boucher, and Marguerite Gérard celebrated the kitten as a tender emblem of private boudoir life and sentimental comfort.

name: British Georgian & Satirical Painting
introduction: In Georgian London, William Hogarth used the predatory cat to puncture aristocratic innocence, while Gainsborough and Stubbs observed domestic pets with sensitive English naturalism.

name: Romanticism & Realism
introduction: Delacroix and Géricault drew the domestic cat to unlock the raw anatomy of wild felines, paving the way for Courbet and Manet to use the cat as a provocative herald of Parisian realism.

name: Victorian & Academic Cat Portraiture
introduction: Led by the acclaimed Belgian-Dutch master Henriëtte Ronner-Knip alongside Couldery, Dolph, and Brunel-Neuville, nineteenth-century academic painters elevated feline portraiture to a celebrated fine art discipline.

name: Impressionism
introduction: Renoir, Cassatt, Morisot, and Degas integrated cats into the sunlit fabric of modern domestic life, painting furry companions resting in girls' laps and sleeping on plush velvet chairs.

name: Post-Impressionism
introduction: Post-Impressionists and Nabis like Bonnard, Gauguin, and Van Gogh simplified form and deepened color, using elongated feline curves and mysterious silhouetted postures to evoke mood.

name: Symbolism, Posters & Art Nouveau
introduction: Montmartre's cabaret culture and Art Nouveau decorative arts embraced the cat as an icon of Bohemian freedom, seen in Steinlen's legendary posters, Louis Wain's anthropomorphic comedies, and Beardsley's sinister lines.

name: American Folk, Naive Art & Popular Prints
introduction: Self-taught itinerant limners, ceramic makers, and printmakers celebrated cats in bold, flat patterns: wide-eyed calicos in provincial parlors and satirical Russian lubki mocking state power.

name: Nineteenth-Century Book Illustration
introduction: A practice-driven movement encompassing wood engraving, steel engraving, and lithographic illustration produced for printed books and periodicals, flourishing across Europe and America as advances in printing technology met rising literacy and demand for illustrated literature.

name: Fauvism & Expressionism
introduction: Der Blaue Reiter and German Expressionists, above all Franz Marc, explored animal purity as a spiritual antidote to industrialized humanity, painting cats in radiant primary colors and rhythmic geometric planes.

name: Early Modernism, Ashcan & New Objectivity
introduction: From Gwen John's delicate Parisian portraits and Tsuguharu Foujita's milk-white glazed felines to Paul Klee's psychological abstraction, early modernists saw the cat as an emblem of modern solitude and pure graphic line.

name: École de Paris
introduction: École de Paris refers to the community of French and émigré artists working in Paris in the first half of the twentieth century.

name: Modern Chinese Painting
introduction: Early twentieth-century Chinese painting that reformed traditional ink practice through Western academic realism, championed by Xu Beihong and his contemporaries.

name: Młoda Polska (Young Poland)
introduction: Młoda Polska (Young Poland) was a Polish modernist movement (c. 1890–1918) synthesising Symbolism, Art Nouveau, and early modernism across literature, music, and the visual arts.

name: South American Pre-Columbian Art
introduction: Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú, Calima, and Inca artists immortalized pampas cats, pumas, and jaguars in textiles, stirrup-spout vessels, gold, and monumental geoglyphs across the Andes and northern South America.

name: Mesoamerican & Central American Art
introduction: Olmec, Teotihuacan, Maya, and Diquís artists rendered jaguars and other felines as shamanic alter egos, celestial guardians, and emblems of rulership in jade, murals, polychrome ceramics, and cast gold.

name: Ancient Near East & Levantine Antiquities
introduction: Mesopotamian, Elamite, Anatolian, and Indus Valley artifacts capturing felines in bronze standards, carved cylinder seals, and architectural portal sculpture.

name: Viking & Early Scandinavian Art
introduction: Zoomorphic woodcarvings and silver amulets from Oseberg and Birka connecting felines with Nordic mythology and the chariot of Freyja.

name: Surrealism & Mid-Century Modernism
introduction: Surrealist, Existentialist, and postwar painters and sculptors (Picasso, Giacometti, Kahlo, Carrington) explored the cat as an occult guardian and solitary witness.

name: Expressionism
introduction: Art that distorts form and colour to convey inner feeling over outward appearance, from Die Brücke in Dresden and Der Blaue Reiter in Munich to Vienna and Berlin. Cats appear as intimate, restless companions rendered in saturated colour and bold, angular line.

name: Ming Dynasty Court & Literati Painting
introduction: Imperial and scholar-official painting during the Ming dynasty, characterized by refined animalier studies and poetic garden observations.

name: Late Twentieth Century & Contemporary Art
introduction: From 1960 through the 21st century, the domestic feline evolved from an intimate household companion into a universal icon of Pop Art, visionary folk painting, public civic sculpture, and digital culture.

name: Old & Middle Kingdom Art & Tomb Reliefs
introduction: From Fifth Dynasty Saqqara tomb reliefs to Eleventh and Twelfth Dynasty painted tombs at Beni Hasan and turquoise faience amulets, Middle Kingdom Egyptian art documents the earliest named domestic felines (miw) and their roles as hunters and companions.

name: Second Intermediate & Early New Kingdom Jewellery
introduction: During the Seventeenth Dynasty at Thebes, royal goldsmiths created magnificent solid gold spacer-bars and cuff bracelets featuring couchant cats bearing the cartouches of King Intef and Queen Sobekemsaf.

name: Pop Art, Visionary Folk & Contemporary Art
introduction: Contemporary artists celebrate felines across bold acrylics, public bronze monuments, graphic comix, and digital media.

name: South, Himalayan & Southeast Asian Art
introduction: Across the Indian subcontinent, the Himalayas, and Southeast Asia, felines feature prominently in Buddhist Jataka reliefs, Hindu devotional art of Shashti, royal Siamese treatise manuscripts (Tamra Maew), and Kalighat folk paintings.
